title: PV Function: Present Value of a Future Sum or a Payment Stream
description: PV present value discounts a future lump sum or a stream of payments back to today, plus the sign rule, four traps and the Excel-to-Sheets differences.
intro: $50,000 promised in five years is not a $50,000 decision today. At 6% a year that promise is worth $37,068.61 right now, and that is the number any savings plan or purchase should be measured against. PV does the discount in one function, including the messier case of a payment arriving every month for years.
prerequisites: A spreadsheet with a rate, a term and an amount to work with
Comfort with cell references and the percent sign
Willingness to type a negative number for money leaving your account

sections.title: The $50,000 That Is Not Worth $50,000 Today
sections.content: A savings goal sits in a single cell: 50000, dated five years out. The rate on the account is 6% a year, compounded monthly. Type =PV(0.005,60,0,50000) and Excel returns ($37,068.61). The parentheses are Excel's way of writing a negative, and the sign is correct here: $37,068.61 leaves your account today so that $50,000 can arrive in 2031. The $12,931.39 between the two figures is interest, not a discount you negotiated. Nothing about the formula depends on today's date. PV only knows that five years is 60 periods and that each period earns half a percent.

example.explanation: 6% a year is 0.5% a month and five years is 60 months. No money is added along the way, so pmt is 0 and the whole answer comes from discounting the 50000 in fv. Double the goal to 100000 and the result doubles exactly to ($74,137.22), a straight line that stops holding the moment a pmt enters the formula.

tips: Leave fv out and there is nothing to discount: =PV(0.005,60,0) returns 0, which is correct and rarely what the person typing it wanted.
Confirm the direction with =FV(0.005,60,0,-37068.61). It returns $50,000.00, which is the whole point of the pair.
Rate and nper have to describe the same period. 6 with 60 periods returns 83.33, a small number that looks like a result and means nothing.

sections.title: Syntax, the Sign Rule, and the Argument People Skip
sections.content: The signature is PV(rate, nper, pmt, [fv], [type]). It mirrors FV almost argument for argument, which is why the two get confused: FV asks what a balance grows into, PV asks what a future balance is worth now. Both treat money leaving your pocket as negative, so a deposit plan produces a positive PV and a loan produces a negative one. Excel accepts at most five arguments, and the last two are optional only in the sense that a missing pmt is read as 0 and a missing type as 0.

steps.name: Convert the annual rate to a period rate
steps.text: Divide by the number of compounding periods in a year. Monthly means 12, and the cell should show 0.005 rather than 0.5.

steps.name: Count periods, not years
steps.text: Five years of monthly periods is 60. A 30-year mortgage is 360, which is where most people first notice that nper is not a year count.

steps.name: Enter outflows as negative
steps.text: If the money leaves your account, put a minus in front. Mixed signs are the single most common reason a PV result looks wrong.

steps.name: Decide on type only when a pmt exists
steps.text: 0 pays at the end of each period and 1 at the start. With pmt at 0 the argument changes nothing, which surprises people who set it and see an identical result.

example.explanation: The same goal funded monthly instead of in one lump. Sixty deposits of $716.64 total $42,998.40, which is $5,929.79 more than the $37,068.61 lump sum, because each deposit arrives later and earns less interest.

tips: fv and pmt can both be supplied at once: =PV(0.005,60,-500,-50000) returns $62,931.39, the sum of the payment stream and the lump sum discounted separately.
Text in any numeric argument returns #VALUE!, including a number pasted from a PDF as text.
PV has no lock on the rate. Drop 0.005 to 0.0025 and the same $50,000 goal costs $43,043.46 today, because less interest does the work for you along the way.

sections.title: Valuing a Stream of Payments
sections.content: Sixty deposits of $500 add up to $30,000 of your own money. At 6% a year that stream is worth $25,862.78 today, so $4,137.22 of the total is interest the lump sum would earn while the deposits trickle in. The rate is the sensitivity dial. Hold the payments fixed and move the rate: 3% a year gives $27,826.18, 12% a year gives $22,477.52. Same 60 payments, a spread of $5,348.66 between the two, and none of it comes from changing the amount you save.

example.explanation: pmt is negative because the $500 leaves your account each month, so PV comes back positive: the lump sum that produces the identical 60 payments. Flip pmt to positive 500 and the answer becomes ($25,862.78) with nothing else changed.

steps.name: Pay at the start of the period
steps.text: Deposits made on the first of the month earn interest for that month. type=1 lifts the value to $25,992.09, a gain of $129.31 that costs nothing but a payroll date.

steps.name: Prove type does nothing without pmt
steps.text: With pmt at 0 the answer stays $37,068.61 whether type is 0 or 1, because type scales the payment annuity and there is no annuity. People spend an afternoon on this one.

steps.name: Sanity-check with a zero rate
steps.text: At rate 0 there is no discounting, so PV returns the plain sum of the payments. If this does not equal 30000, one of the other arguments is wrong.

tips: Ten years of the same $500 is worth $45,036.73, well short of double $25,862.78. Later payments are discounted harder, so duration buys value at a falling rate.
A 12% discount rate is not a forecast. It is an assumption about what else the money could earn, so run 3%, 6% and 8% before signing a lease or a purchase.
The account that pays 12% is not the same account that pays 6%. Mixing a quoted rate with the wrong compounding frequency is how the inputs drift apart.

sections.title: Reading a Loan Backwards
sections.content: A $200,000 mortgage at 6% over 30 years carries a payment of $1,199.10. Feed that payment back into PV and you get $199,999.82 instead of $200,000. The missing 18 cents is rounding: PMT returned 1199.1010, the cents version is slightly low, and 360 of those tiny shortfalls add up to 18 cents. After 60 payments there are 300 left, so =PV(0.005,300,-1199.10) returns $186,108.55, the balance still owed at the five-year mark. Payments by then total $71,946, and only $13,891.45 of it touched the principal.

example.explanation: The remaining payments are all the balance is: discount 300 of them and the answer is what you still owe. Drop nper to 1 to see the payoff figure one month before the end, which is the deposit the final payment has to clear.

steps.name: Build the payment from the principal
steps.text: PMT and PV are inverses. Start with the loan amount, get the payment, then feed that payment back into PV and watch it return the amount you started with.

steps.name: Take the balance at any point
steps.text: Subtract the payments already made from nper. Five years in, that is 360 minus 60, and the result is the payoff principal on that date.

steps.name: Separate principal from interest
steps.text: Subtract the balance from the original loan to get the principal repaid. Everything else you paid was interest, and on a 30-year loan that is the larger half for a long time.

tips: This is the arithmetic behind an amortization schedule. Checking one row of the lender's table against PV is the fastest way to confirm the schedule is right.
NPER works the other way: =NPER(0.005,-1199.10,200000) returns 360.0009 rather than a clean 360, the same 18-cent rounding showing up as a fraction of a payment.
A payoff quote that is a few dollars off the PV result usually means the lender is adding per-diem interest to the date of the wire. The function is not wrong.

sections.title: PV vs NPV, and Where Excel and Google Sheets Split
sections.content: PV assumes every payment is the same size. Real projects do not pay evenly, so NPV takes a range instead: =NPV(0.06,3000,4000,5000) returns $10,588.27. The catch is timing. NPV discounts the first value by a full period, so an outlay made today belongs outside the function: =-10000+NPV(0.06,3000,4000,5000) gives $588.27. Put the -10000 inside the range and you get $1,154.31, an overstatement of $566.04 that has sunk more project approvals than any other spreadsheet mistake.

example.explanation: Ten thousand spent now, then 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 over the next three years. The project clears its 6% hurdle by $588.27, which is thin enough that a different discount rate flips the decision. The break-even rate for these flows, what IRR reports, is 8.90%.

steps.name: See the timing error for yourself
steps.text: Moving the outlay inside the range discounts it too, as if it were spent a year from now, and inflates the answer by 600/1.06.

steps.name: Cross-check the rate with RATE
steps.text: Given a PV of 25,862.78, a payment of -500 and 60 periods, RATE returns 0.5%. If your inputs disagree with the rate you assumed, one of the three is wrong.

steps.name: Use XNPV when the dates are uneven
steps.text: Quarterly or annual flows on real calendar dates need the date range passed alongside the values, because XNPV discounts by actual days rather than by period count.

tips: Google Sheets takes the same five arguments in the same order, though its documentation names them rate, number_of_periods, payment_amount, future_value and end_or_beginning. Every formula on this page returns the same figure in both apps.
NPV in Sheets behaves identically, including the one-period shift on the first value, so the fix travels with the file.
Neither function knows about fees, tax or inflation. Fold them into the discount rate deliberately, and write the assumption into a cell so the next person can see it.

functionsUsed.name: PV
functionsUsed.description: PV returns the current value of a future stream of cash flows discounted at a constant rate.

functionsUsed.name: FV
functionsUsed.description: FV returns the future value of an investment based on periodic, constant payments and a constant interest rate.

functionsUsed.name: PMT
functionsUsed.description: PMT calculates the periodic payment for a loan or investment based on constant payments and a constant interest rate. It's the function you need for mortgage, car loan, and any fixed-rate payment calculations.

functionsUsed.name: RATE
functionsUsed.description: RATE returns the periodic interest rate for an annuity based on the number of periods, payment amount, present value, and future value.

functionsUsed.name: NPER
functionsUsed.description: NPER returns the total number of payment periods required to reach a target value given a fixed interest rate and payment.

functionsUsed.name: NPV
functionsUsed.description: NPV calculates the net present value of an investment based on a discount rate and a series of future cash flows.

summary: PV turns a future amount into today's money: divide the annual rate by the compounding periods, count the periods, and put a minus sign on anything that leaves your account. Use fv for a single future sum, pmt for a repeating payment, and both when a plan has a lump sum and a deposit schedule. Type 1 only matters when a payment exists, and a rate of 0 is a useful check that the other arguments add up. Reach for NPV once the flows stop being equal, keeping today's outlay outside the range. The trade-off is that every one of these answers is only as good as the rate you typed, so treat the rate as an assumption on the sheet rather than a fact.
